title: SDLC and CI/CD on Google Cloud
bodyMarkdown:
## Why this matters for the PCA exam

The "Analyzing and optimizing technical and business processes" domain carries about 15% of the exam, and the first sub-objective is analyzing and defining technical processes: the SDLC, CI/CD, root-cause analysis and disaster recovery. For CI/CD the exam rarely asks for syntax. It gives you a team with manual, error-prone releases and asks which combination of managed services, controls and practices fixes that. The winning answer almost always automates the path to production, keeps what was tested identical to what ships, adds a human or policy gate where risk justifies it, and makes rollback cheap.

## The SDLC as a feedback loop

A healthy SDLC is not a one-way conveyor: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, then feed telemetry and incidents back into planning. Your job as an architect is to shorten that loop without removing safety. The industry yardstick is the set of DORA software delivery metrics. [DORA](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/) groups five of them into two families:

| Family | Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput | Change lead time | Time from commit to version control until deployed in production |
| Throughput | Deployment frequency | Deployments over a period, or time between deployments |
| Throughput | Failed deployment recovery time | Time to recover from a deployment that fails and needs immediate intervention |
| Stability | Change fail rate | Share of deployments needing immediate intervention, typically a rollback or hotfix |
| Stability | Deployment rework rate | Share of deployments that are unplanned and result from a production incident |

DORA's point is that throughput and stability move together: top performers do well across all five, so "slow down to be safe" is rarely the right answer. Smaller, more frequent, automated releases lower the blast radius of each change.

## The reference Google Cloud pipeline

| Stage | Service | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Source and trigger | GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Cloud Source Repositories, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or webhooks | Cloud Build triggers on commits, pull requests, tags or events |
| Build and test | Cloud Build | Each step runs in a container; YAML or JSON config; private pools for private-network access |
| Artifact store | Artifact Registry | Containers plus language and OS packages; replaces Container Registry |
| Gate | Binary Authorization | Admits only images carrying required attestations |
| Deliver | Cloud Deploy | Ordered targets, promotion, approvals, canary, verification, rollback |
| Operate | Cloud Monitoring, Logging, Trace | Closes the loop and drives verification and alerts |

### Cloud Build

Per the [Cloud Build overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/overview), builds run as steps, each in its own container, defined in a YAML or JSON build configuration. It can be triggered from Cloud Source Repositories, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, Bitbucket, Cloud Storage, and Pub/Sub or webhook events. **Private pools** are dedicated worker pools that scale automatically and can reach resources in a private network; choose them when the build must touch a private database, an internal package mirror or on-premises systems over VPN.

Step ordering matters for speed. Per [the build step order guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/configure-build-step-order), a step with no `waitFor` waits for all prior steps to succeed, so the default is sequential. A step that waits on `-` starts immediately when the build starts, and listing step IDs creates a dependency graph. Running lint, unit tests and image build in parallel is the cheap way to shorten feedback time.

Cloud Build's features meet SLSA level 3 requirements and can generate provenance for container images, and it integrates with Binary Authorization so that deployments of images not produced by Cloud Build can be blocked.

### Artifact Registry

[Artifact Registry](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/overview) is the recommended container registry on Google Cloud. It stores Docker images, Helm charts, Go, Java, Node.js, Python, Ruby and Conda packages, Debian and RPM packages, and generic artifacts, and integrates with Artifact Analysis for container vulnerability scanning. Container Registry is gone: per the [transition guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/transition/transition-from-gcr), it was shut down effective March 18, 2025, and `gcr.io` URLs hosted on Artifact Registry are not affected. So any answer that pushes images to Container Registry is wrong.

Location choice is a trade-off. The [location documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/repositories/repo-locations) says a single region optimizes latency and bandwidth for consumers in the same region, while a multi-region may keep working if one of its regions is down. The catch: operations in multi-region repositories may be slower, and if a multi-region repository has an operational failure, all its users are affected regardless of region. For GKE Image Streaming, the repository must be in the same region as your nodes or in a corresponding multi-region.

### Cloud Deploy

[Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) automates delivery "to a series of target environments in a defined promotion sequence". The vocabulary the exam uses:

- **Delivery pipeline:** the promotion sequence of targets, for example dev, staging, prod.
- **Target:** an environment: GKE, Cloud Run or GKE attached clusters. Cloud Deploy uses Skaffold for rendering, deployment and verification.
- **Release:** the rendered manifest for each target.
- **Rollout:** the deployment of a release to one target. Each promotion creates a new rollout.
- **Rollback:** triggering a rollout of the last successfully deployed release.

## Approvals, verification and progressive delivery

### Approvals as change management

Setting `requireApproval: true` on a target makes a rollout wait for a human. Per the [approvals documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/promote-release), any user or service account with `roles/clouddeploy.approver` can approve, and a rejected rollout is not deployed and cannot be approved later unless it is re-promoted. Cloud Deploy also publishes Pub/Sub notifications for render, deploy and approval events, which is how you page an approver or post to chat.

Be careful not to over-apply this. DORA's research on [change approval](https://dora.dev/capabilities/streamlining-change-approval/) found that heavyweight external change approval boards had a negative impact on software delivery performance, with no evidence they lowered change fail rate. The recommended pattern is peer review captured in the development platform plus automated testing and monitoring. Use a manual approval gate for production or regulated targets, not as a substitute for automation.

### Verification and canary

[Deployment strategies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies) in Cloud Deploy are **standard** (deploy straight to the target) and **canary** (deploy first to a portion of the infrastructure, test, then roll out further). Both support all Cloud Deploy runtimes. Percentages must be whole numbers, so 20.5% is not allowed. On the first deployment to a target there is nothing to compare against, so the rollout may skip canary phases.

[Verification](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/verify-deployment) runs after deployment in the Cloud Deploy execution environment. Success is the container exit code: `0` is success and non-zero is failure, and if verification fails, the rollout fails. For GKE you can run verification on the application cluster, but Cloud Run deployments can only verify from the Cloud Deploy execution environment.

[Automation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/automation) can auto-promote after a successful rollout, promote on a cron schedule, advance canary phases, and repair failed rollouts by retrying and then, when attempts are exhausted, creating a rollout back to the most recent successful release.

### Supply-chain gate

[Binary Authorization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) enforces a policy of rules over container images on GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Service Mesh and Google Distributed Cloud. An attestation is a signed record of the image's registry path and digest, for example produced by Cloud Build or by a manual QA sign-off. Two operational features show up in scenarios: **dry-run** logs violations without blocking, which is how you introduce a policy safely, and **breakglass** lets authorized people bypass enforcement during an incident, with audit logs recording why an image was out of compliance.

## Choosing the right gate

| Situation | Best control |
|---|---|
| Images must come only from your trusted build | Binary Authorization with a Cloud Build attestation |
| Production needs human sign-off | `requireApproval` plus the approver role on the prod target |
| Need to limit blast radius of a bad release | Canary with verification and repair or rollback automation |
| Build must reach private resources | Cloud Build private pool |
| Introducing a new policy to existing teams | Dry-run first, then enforce |
| Infra changes need review | Plan in CI, policy check, approval, then apply |

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Rebuilding per environment.** Building a fresh image for staging and again for prod breaks the guarantee that what was tested is what ships. Build once, promote the same artifact by digest.
- **Using Container Registry or Cloud Storage as an image store.** Container Registry is shut down; use Artifact Registry.
- **Human-only gates everywhere.** Mandatory manual approval for every environment turns CI/CD back into a ticket queue and, per DORA, does not reduce change failures.
- **No rollback path.** A pipeline with no tested rollback or automatic repair converts every bad release into an incident.
- **Enforcing Binary Authorization on day one.** Without dry-run you can block legitimate deployments, then teams adopt breakglass as the norm.
- **Deploying straight to production from a laptop.** It bypasses review, audit trail and verification, and is the standard distractor for "manual hotfix" options.
- **Disabling monitoring during releases.** Verification and canary analysis need telemetry; silencing it removes the signal.
- **Multi-region artifact repositories for everything.** They can be slower and share a failure domain; match location to where builds and clusters run.

## Exam tips

- **Canonical chain:** Cloud Build to Artifact Registry to Cloud Deploy, observed with Cloud Monitoring and Logging. If an option uses Compute Engine startup scripts, Filestore or Container Registry for CI/CD, eliminate it.
- **Container Registry is shut down.** Artifact Registry is the answer for images and packages; `gcr.io` hostnames hosted on Artifact Registry keep working.
- **Approval gates belong on production and regulated targets.** In Cloud Deploy that is `requireApproval` plus `roles/clouddeploy.approver`; a rejected rollout must be re-promoted.
- **Safe release equals canary plus verification plus rollback.** Cloud Deploy canary uses whole-number percentages, verification fails the rollout on a non-zero exit code, and rollback redeploys the last successful release.
- **Trusted artifacts:** Cloud Build provenance plus Binary Authorization attestations; use dry-run to introduce policy and breakglass only for emergencies.
- **Validate infrastructure like code.** Terraform plan, policy check, review, then apply; unit and integration tests run as Cloud Build steps on every commit.
- **Reject risky options.** "Push hotfixes directly to production," "skip staging to save cost," and "disable monitoring during releases" are always wrong.
- **DORA framing:** high performers improve throughput and stability together, so small frequent automated releases beat large infrequent gated ones.

flowchart LR
  Dev["Commit or pull request"] --> CB["Cloud Build: build and test"]
  CB --> AR["Artifact Registry: image"]
  CB --> Att["Attestation and provenance"]
  AR --> CD["Cloud Deploy pipeline"]
  Att --> BA{"Binary Authorization policy"}
  CD --> DevT["Dev target"]
  DevT --> Stg["Staging target"]
  Stg --> Appr{"Prod approval"}
  Appr --> BA
  BA -->|"Compliant"| Prod["Prod: canary then full"]
  BA -->|"Blocked"| Stop["Deployment denied"]
  Prod --> Ops["Monitoring and Logging feedback"]

sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Developer
  participant CB as Cloud Build

  participant CD as Cloud Deploy

  participant Prod as Prod target
  Dev->>CB: Push commit
  CB->>AR: Push tested image
  CB->>CD: Create release
  CD->>CD: Auto promote dev and staging

  CD->>Prod: Canary phase
  Prod-->>CD: Verification exit code

    CD->>Prod: Repair, retry then roll back
